title: Blog
text:
Paying for wins


Two web pages, 348 players, and the worst place in the NBA to spend money


Scraping Basketball-Reference salaries and production to find out which part of the market sells a win cheapest. It is not the part teams spend most in.





Sep 21, 2026


Kyle Tong












The average that disagrees with all of its parts


Simpson’s paradox, and why ratios refuse to add up


Berkeley’s 1973 admissions gap disappears once you look at departments. The arithmetic behind that is simple, and it is a trap you can walk into with any pooled comparison.





Sep 12, 2026


Kyle Tong





No matching items

title: The average that disagrees with all of its parts
text:
In 1973 the graduate school at Berkeley admitted about 44% of men who applied and about 30% of women. Thousands of applicants sit behind those two numbers, so the gap is not noise. Split the same applicants by department and it very nearly disappears. In the largest department of all, women were admitted at a higher rate than men.
Nothing was recounted. The two statements are about the same people.

title: The average that disagrees with all of its parts
section: What the Berkeley numbers look like
text:
What the Berkeley numbers look like
R ships with the data, so you can check this in four lines.

rates <- as.data.frame(UCBAdmissions) |>
  group_by(Dept, Gender) |>
  summarise(applicants = sum(Freq),
            admitted   = sum(Freq[Admit == "Admitted"]),
            .groups    = "drop") |>
  mutate(rate = admitted / applicants)

rates |>
  select(Dept, Gender, applicants, rate) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Gender, values_from = c(applicants, rate)) |>
  transmute(Department    = Dept,
            `Men applied` = applicants_Male,
            `Men admitted` = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * rate_Male),
            `Women applied` = applicants_Female,
            `Women admitted` = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * rate_Female)) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrrr")

Departments A and B admitted more than 60% of everyone who applied. Departments C through F admitted far fewer. Men applied overwhelmingly to A and B; women applied overwhelmingly to C through F.

pooled <- rates |>
  group_by(Gender) |>
  summarise(rate = sum(admitted) / sum(applicants))

ggplot(rates, aes(Dept, rate, colour = Gender)) +
  geom_hline(data = pooled, aes(yintercept = rate, colour = Gender),
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(aes(size = applicants)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 8) +
  labs(x = "department", y = "admission rate", colour = NULL, size = "applicants")







Figure 1: Admission rate by department and gender. Point size is the number of applicants. Dashed lines are the pooled rates.





The dashed lines are far apart. The points are not.

title: The average that disagrees with all of its parts
text:
Why ratios can do this
A pooled rate is a weighted average of the department rates,
\[
\bar r = \sum_d w_d \, r_d, \qquad w_d = \frac{n_d}{\sum_k n_k},
\]
and the weights \(w_d\) are part of the data, not a constant you can divide out. Men and women faced the same \(r_d\) but carried different \(w_d\), and the difference in weights is bigger than the differences in rates. Pooling therefore measures something nobody intended to measure: where each group chose to apply.

title: The average that disagrees with all of its parts
text:
Why it feels impossible
Counts behave the way intuition expects. If men outnumber women in every department, they outnumber women overall, always. We quietly extend that rule to percentages, and for percentages it is false. Adding a fraction to a fraction means adding numerators and denominators separately, and the denominators are free to move.
The phenomenon predates its name by half a century. Pearson noticed in 1899 that mixing two populations manufactures correlations that exist in neither, and Yule gave the contingency-table version in 1903. Simpson’s 1951 paper worked out what the reversal means for interpreting interaction, and Blyth attached his name to it in 1972. Yule had it first, which is why some writers call it the Yule-Simpson effect.
One thing the Berkeley example does not show is that there was no discrimination. Bickel and his coauthors, writing in Science in 1975, made that point themselves: conditioning on department moves the question rather than closing it, since departments differ in funding and capacity, and applicants do not choose where to apply in a vacuum.

title: The average that disagrees with all of its parts
text:
Takeaway
A pooled comparison is an average, and an average has weights. When two groups are averaged with different weights, the pooled numbers can point the opposite way from every group inside them. Before you read anything into a headline rate, find out what is being averaged and how the weights differ. The reversal is not a rare pathology; it is what happens whenever composition and outcome are related.
Admissions counts are UCBAdmissions in R’s datasets package, from Bickel, Hammel and O’Connell (1975), Science 187, 398–404.

Welcome to my personal website.

Quick Links

title: Paying for wins
text: A team with $30 million of cap space this October can buy about 4.2 points of VORP with it, or about 1.5, depending entirely on which part of the salary market it shops in. VORP is Basketball-Reference’s value over replacement player, and multiplying by 2.7 turns it into wins, so the gap between those two numbers is about 7 wins for the same money.

title: Paying for wins
text:
Getting the data
Basketball-Reference publishes last season’s player statistics and next season’s contracts as ordinary HTML tables. There is no API and no bulk download for them, which is what puts this in scraping territory. Their robots.txt blocks game logs, splits and lineups but leaves /leagues/ and /contracts/ open, and asks for a three second crawl delay, so the acquisition script sends two requests four seconds apart, identifies itself in the user agent, and saves the HTML to disk.

page <- read_html("https://www.basketball-reference.com/leagues/NBA_2026_advanced.html")
xml2::write_html(page, "data/raw/bbref_advanced_2026.html")

advanced <- page |>
  html_element("#advanced") |>
  html_table()

Saving the snapshot matters more than it looks. Every later step parses the local file, so fixing a bug costs zero additional requests, and if the site redesigns its tables next spring the analysis still runs against the page I actually saw.
Two things in the parsed tables would have quietly corrupted the result. Player names carry bracketed footnote markers, so Jokić[a] and Jokić fail to join. And a player traded mid-season gets one row per team plus a combined 2TM row, all sharing a rank, so James Harden appears three times unless the partial rows are dropped. Salaries arrive as strings like $62,587,158, which parse_number() handles.
Because VORP is a fixed function of two other scraped columns, \((\text{BPM} + 2) \times \text{MP} / (48 \times 82)\), recomputing it is a free test of the whole parse. Across 348 players the largest disagreement is rounding, which rules out shifted columns and numbers read as text.

title: Paying for wins
text:
What production costs
Joining production to salary on player name matched 86 percent of contracts. The misses are not spelling errors: they are 2026 draft picks with no NBA minutes and stars who missed all of last season hurt, which is worth remembering when reading anything below about the top of the market.








Figure 1: Total salary divided by total positive VORP, within each salary band. Players with at least 500 minutes in 2025-26, priced against their 2026-27 salary.





Production gets more expensive as salaries rise, which is what competition for scarce talent is supposed to do. The surprise is where the line stops rising. The most expensive production in the league is not at the top: it is in the $15 to $30 million band, at $19.9 million per point, above the $17.3 million that players earning more than $30 million cost.
Two rules explain the shape. At the top, the collective bargaining agreement caps individual salaries, so the best players in the league cannot be paid what they are worth. At the bottom, minimum and rookie scale contracts are set by rule rather than by bidding, and a young player who turns out to be good stays cheap for years. The $15 to $30 million band has neither protection. It is priced by open negotiation for players good enough to be paid but not good enough to be capped, and it is the one place where teams routinely pay full price.

title: Paying for wins
text:
What to do with that
For a team with cap space and no path to a superstar, the advice is to spend at the extremes and stay out of the middle. Four players at $7 million who each produce half a point of VORP return twice what one player at $28 million producing a single point does, for the same money. The limit is the roster: 15 spots and 240 minutes a night, so a team that already has useful cheap players cannot simply buy more of them, and improving a good roster does eventually require paying for production per minute rather than per dollar.
Two caveats. VORP is a box score estimate and misses everything that does not end in a counted event, and the salary is for next season while the production is from last season, which will be wrong about exactly the players who change most.
Both scripts are in R/, the raw HTML snapshots and a provenance record in data/raw/, and the tidy file behind the chart in data/derived/. Only 01_acquire.R touches the network. Data from Basketball-Reference, accessed 20 September 2026.
